title: Inherited Mineral Rights
note: heirs deciding whether to keep or sell
metaTitle: Inherited Mineral Rights in Pennsylvania - What to Do Next
metaDescription: Just inherited Marcellus or Utica mineral rights in Pennsylvania? We'll walk you through the paperwork and give a fair offer, no pressure, family to family.
heroLead: Inheriting mineral rights usually means inheriting a stack of paperwork you didn't ask for, on top of everything else that comes with losing someone.
intro: We inherited our own mineral interest the same way most families in Pennsylvania do - a parent passed, and somewhere in the estate paperwork was a mention of oil and gas rights nobody had thought about in years, tied to land that hadn't been actively farmed in a generation. It's disorienting. You're grieving, you're dealing with an estate, and now there's a decision about a mineral interest layered on top that you never expected to make.

There's no wrong choice here between keeping it and selling it. Some families hold onto inherited minerals because it feels like the last connection to a grandparent's farm, and that's a real and valid reason to keep something. Others would rather convert it to cash and be done with the ongoing paperwork, tax reporting, and occasional operator correspondence. We just want you to make that decision with clear information, not under pressure from a letter that showed up in the mail.

sections.heading: First, Get the Interest Actually Transferred Into Your Name
paragraphs: Before you can sell, or even sign a division order to keep receiving royalty, the mineral interest needs to be legally transferred out of the deceased owner's name and into yours, usually through the probate or estate process and recorded at the county recorder of deeds. If the estate went through probate for other reasons, the mineral interest should have been addressed as part of that, but it's worth double-checking it was actually recorded and not only mentioned in the will.

If probate is still open or hasn't started, that has to happen before a sale can close cleanly. We've walked a number of families through exactly this sequence and can tell you what documentation a title company or attorney will want to see.

sections.heading: Figuring Out What You Actually Inherited
paragraphs: Sometimes it's obvious - a will names a specific mineral interest and a county. Other times it's buried in a residuary clause with everything else, and you have to go dig through old deed records to figure out exactly what formation, what acreage, and what county your family's interest covers. If your relative kept old lease documents, division order statements, or check stubs, those are worth holding onto; they tell us who the operator is and give a starting point for production history.

If there's nothing on paper at all, that's not unusual either, especially for older interests that predate the shale boom and were leased decades before Marcellus drilling made them relevant again. We can usually trace ownership through the county courthouse if you can tell us roughly where the land was.

sections.heading: Weighing Keep vs. Sell Without the Sales Pitch
paragraphs: If the interest is producing and the royalty checks are meaningful, some heirs choose to keep it as ongoing income, understanding that shale wells decline over time and the check five years from now will likely be smaller than it is today. If the interest is scattered among several heirs who all want different things, or if it's a small fractional piece that's more paperwork than it's worth managing, selling and splitting the proceeds is often the simpler path for everyone.

There's also a middle situation we see a lot: one sibling wants to keep the family connection and the others want cash. In that case, some heirs sell their individual undivided shares while another keeps theirs - you don't all have to agree on the same outcome.

sections.heading: What We'll Actually Ask You For
paragraphs: To put together a real offer, we'll want the death certificate, whatever probate or estate documents establish your ownership, and any deed, lease, or division order paperwork you have. If some of that is missing, we can usually help track it down rather than asking you to start from scratch. We move at whatever pace makes sense for you - some families want this resolved quickly during estate settlement, others want to sit with the decision for a while, and both are fine with us.

faqs.question: Do I need to finish probate before I can sell inherited mineral rights?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, the interest needs to be legally transferred into your name through probate and recorded at the county before a sale can close, though we can start the valuation and offer process while that's still underway.

faqs.question: What if multiple siblings inherited the same interest?
faqs.answer: Each heir typically owns an undivided fractional share and can decide independently whether to sell their portion or keep it, regardless of what the others choose.

faqs.question: I don't have any of the original paperwork - can you still help?
faqs.answer: Yes, we can usually trace ownership and lease history through county deed and courthouse records if you can tell us the county and roughly where the land was.

faqs.question: Is it better to sell right after inheriting or wait?
faqs.answer: There's no universal answer - it depends on whether the interest is producing, how the decline curve looks, and what you personally need. We're glad to give you a valuation now even if you decide to wait.

faqs.question: Will selling affect the rest of the estate settlement?
faqs.answer: It shouldn't, as long as the mineral interest has been properly transferred to you individually first. Selling your own inherited share is a separate transaction from the broader estate.
